oom counts the number of times the cgroup's memory usage reached the limit and the allocation was about to fail (a single event, not per process); it is not an OOM-kill count. oom_kill counts processes belonging to this cgroup killed by any kind of OOM killer. An OOM event may kill zero or several processes, and a system-wide OOM can kill this cgroup's processes without this cgroup's own limit being reached, so neither count is a partition or ordering of the other; no containment or order is asserted.

oom counts the number of times the cgroup's memory usage reached the limit and the allocation was about to fail (a single event, not per process). oom_group_kill counts group OOM kills. During a system-wide OOM the OOM killer can select this cgroup's processes and, with memory.oom.group=1, kill the whole group without this cgroup's own memory limit being reached, so oom_group_kill can increase while oom stays zero. oom_group_kill <= oom is therefore not a kernel identity; no containment or order is asserted for this pair.

citations.text: low/high/max/oom/oom_kill/oom_group_kill are cumulative hierarchical event counts unless memory.events.local is used. oom counts the number of times the cgroup's memory usage reached the limit and the allocation was about to fail (a single event, not per process); it is not an OOM-kill count. oom_kill counts processes belonging to this cgroup killed by any kind of OOM killer. oom_group_kill counts the number of times the OOM killer killed all processes belonging to the cgroup (memory.oom.group=1). A group kill selects a victim in this subtree, so under the documented nonempty-victim group-kill assumption oom_group_kill <= oom_kill. The converse, oom_kill <= oom and oom_group_kill <= oom are not asserted: a system-wide OOM can produce a group kill with this cgroup's own oom count zero.

identities.statement: oom_group_kill <= oom_kill for cumulative hierarchical memory.events counters, assuming a group kill has at least one victim; one-way containment only.
